new_statements.quote: Tenyidie is a tonal language and has five tones: High, Mid-High, Mid, Mid-Low and Low. Since Roman script is used for orthographic representation, written Tenyidie does not specify what tone to be used, which is based on the context. Meyase (2016) describes the tone system of Tenyidie as a combination of both Register and Contour tones. In disyllabic words, the first syllable has a register tone while the second has a contour tone. However, in a monosyllabic word, it is register tone [...]. Stress in Tenyidie is realized through elongating the desired syllable while maintaining the tone.
new_statements.citation: Tungoe, Neisakuonuo. 2017. The phonemic inventory of Tenyidie: an acoustic study. PhD thesis (English: Linguistics & Phonetics), The English and Foreign Languages University, Hyderabad. Supervisor C. Meena Debashish.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Tenyidie/Angami is a five-tone (phonetically four-level) language; no positional or lexical word stress is described. The only explicit remark (Tungoe 2017) treats stress as emphatic prominence realized by lengthening whichever syllable the speaker wishes to emphasize, with its lexical tone preserved. Supporting first-hand observations: Kuolie 2004 (2.1.4, p.34) notes word-final vowels are phonetically longer than non-final ones and lists only tone under suprasegmentals; Meyase 2016 (4.4, 5.8) analyses native disyllables as sesquisyllabic - a reduced, toneless initial minor syllable (pe-/te-/the-/ke-/me-/rə-) plus a tone-bearing final major syllable - i.e. structural prominence is root-/word-final, but he never calls it stress.
new_statements.exceptions: None; Tungoe's remark is a single sentence without examples or measurements of stress.
new_statements.domain_note: Tungoe's sentence concerns emphatic/pragmatic stress on a 'desired syllable', not citation-form word stress; Kuolie's final-vowel length remark is phonetic and word-level; Meyase's minor/major syllable asymmetry is defined over the disyllabic prosodic word (prefix/minor syllable + root).
new_statements.identity_note: Tungoe 2017, Kuolie 2004, Meyase 2016 and Terhiija 2024 describe Tenyidie = the Kohima (standard) variety of Angami (anga1288, no separate dialect code needed). Chase 1992 and Blankenship et al. 1993 describe the Khonoma (Khwunomia) dialect of Angami; STEDT Monograph 3 has separate Khonoma and Kohima entries.

sources.note: Ch.II Phonology: 2.3.0 Suprasegmentals lists only the five tones; 2.1.4 (p.34) 'Phonetically final vowels in Tenyidie are usually longer than the non-final vowels... in case emphasis and stress in an intonation patterns, it is much distinctive'; tone contrast of disyllables is concentrated on the final syllable, initial syllable 'regular'. No word-stress rule.

sources.citation: Meyase, Savio Megolhuto. 2016. A morphological investigation of the tonal phonology of Tenyidie. PhD thesis, EFLU Hyderabad (Shodhganga 10603/329839).
sources.note: Chs.1,2,4,5,6 read. 4.4: all monomorphemic disyllables are sesquisyllabic - initial minor syllable (pe-, te-, the-, ke-, me-, rə-) is phonologically reduced and lexically toneless (default Mid), final major syllable carries the lexical tone; 5.8 prosodic word = (σ σ) with M + unpredictable T. No explicit statement about stress.

sources.citation: Blankenship, B., P. Ladefoged, P. Bhaskararao & N. Chase. 1993. Phonetic structures of Khonoma Angami. Linguistics of the Tibeto-Burman Area 16(2): 69-88.
sources.note: Image-only scan, scanned (300 dpi). Vowels, four tones with F0 means, consonants (voiceless nasals etc.). Nothing on stress.

sources.citation: Chase, Nichumeno. 1992. Descriptive analysis of Khwunomia dialect. PhD thesis, Deccan College / University of Poona (Shodhganga 10603/149199).
sources.note: Ch.1 Phonology: 1.2.0 four level tones, 'one-to-one corelation between the number of syllables and the number of tonemes'; 1.5 syllable structure; word lengths 1-5 syllables. Silent on stress.

sources.citation: Giridhar, P. P. 1980. Angami Grammar. Mysore: Central Institute of Indian Languages (archive.org dli.language.0006).
sources.note: 1.0.1 Tones: 'Angami is a non-restricted tone language', five tones (some speakers four); syllable structure p.17 ('minimum requirement for an Angami syllable is a vowel with a concomitant tone'). No mention of stress or accent anywhere.

sources.citation: McCabe, R. B. 1887. Outline grammar of the Angami Naga language. Calcutta: Superintendent of Government Printing (archive.org dli.csl.8027).
sources.note: Uses 'accent, or emphasis' to mean tone ('I have not attempted to mark tones, or emphasis'); no word-stress rule.

sources.citation: Meyase, Savio M. 2024. Dissimilation and phonological conspiracy in Tenyidie tone. Journal of Linguistics. doi:10.1017/S0022226724000392
sources.note: Roots are single CV/CrV syllables; non-compound words max three syllables (up to two Mid-toned prefixes + root). Tone only; no stress statement.

sources.citation: Terhiija, Viyazonuo. 2024. Phonetics of Angami. PhD thesis, IIT Guwahati (Shodhganga 10603/594092), 373 pp.
sources.note: Full acoustic study of nasals, fricatives, affricates, vowels, five tones and tonal coarticulation; searched whole text: no statement on word stress (only generic typology remarks on accentual tone systems).

sources.citation: Meyase, Savio M. 2021. Polarity in a four-level tone language: tone features in Tenyidie. Phonology 38(1): 123-146. doi:10.1017/S0952675721000063
sources.note: Four level lexical tones plus a fifth H+floating M; suffix tonology. Nothing on stress.
